extra.message: Hardcoded Default JWT Secret Key — Attacker can forge arbitrary JWTs to impersonate any user including ops_admin, gaining full system access [verified: backend/app/config.py line 7 defaults SECRET_KEY to 'change-me-in-production-32-char-key!!' when the env var is absent; no startup check or environment gate prevents its use in production, and the key directly signs all JWT tokens in auth.py (lines 31, 37), enabling forgery of tokens for any role including ops_admin.]

Privilege Escalation via Unrestricted Role at Registration — Attacker gains full ops_admin access, bypassing all role-based access controls across the platform. [verified: RegisterRequest accepts role: UserRole with default customer but the register endpoint (auth.py:28) applies zero server-side role restriction — req.role is written directly to user.role with no authorization check. An attacker sends {"role":"ops_admin"} in the public POST /api/auth/register body and creates a super-admin account.]

Path Traversal in SPA Catch-All Route — An unauthenticated attacker can read arbitrary files from the server filesystem including configuration files, environment files, and source code. [verified: User-controlled {path:path} URL segment flows unsanitized into os.path.join(frontend_build, path) then FileResponse; no os.path.realpath confinement or path-sanitization check exists. Attackers can traverse out of the dist directory with ../../../ sequences to read arbitrary server files.]

Password Reset Token Not Invalidated After Use — An attacker who intercepts a password reset token (even after the victim has already used it) can reset the password again and take over the account. [verified: password_reset_confirm (auth.py:108) decodes the JWT but never queries or marks PasswordResetToken as used — the model exists (models.py:325) yet is never instantiated, stored, or checked anywhere. The same JWT stays valid for its full 1-hour lifetime and can reset the password repeatedly after a victim has already used it.]

Hardcoded Default Password for CSV-Imported Users — Any customer imported via CSV can be logged into with a known default password until the password is changed, enabling mass account takeover. [verified: The CSV customer import endpoint at /api/imports/customers (reachable, registered in main.py:54) creates users with bcrypt-hashed password 'changeme123' — a trivially guessable hardcoded default. No forced-password-change mechanism or must_change flag exists anywhere in the codebase, so any imported customer who doesn't proactively change their password is immediately compromisable via credential ]

Internal Notes Exposed to Customer-Role Users — Customers can read internal-only operational notes containing sensitive dispatch information, incident handling details, and internal job commentary [verified: get_job returns JobOut (schemas.py:206) which includes internal_notes; can_access_job (dependencies.py:22-39) only checks ownership, never strips the field, and no middleware or response filtering exists.]

Missing authorization: customers can access any route by ID, exposing cross-customer job data — An authenticated customer can enumerate route IDs and retrieve full route details including stops with their associated jobs, leaking internal_notes, customer identities, worker assignments, and service details across the entire platform. [verified: The get_route endpoint uses get_current_user (not require_roles), has authorization checks only for field_worker and dispatcher roles, and has no branch for customer — customers fall through to return the full RouteOut with nested JobOut data including internal_notes, cross-customer job details, and worker assignments. The list_routes and list_jobs endpoints both properly restrict customers, confi]

IDOR: Unauthorized Access to Worker Job Listings — Cross-role access to sensitive job assignment data of any field worker, leaking operational information to unauthorized users [verified: Endpoint uses get_current_user (auth only, no role gate) and only restricts field_worker to own profile; customers and other roles bypass the single if-guard entirely, allowing any authenticated user to retrieve all jobs for any worker_id with full field exposure including internal_notes.]

Sensitive Bearer Token Logged in Application Logs — Bearer tokens captured in logs can be exfiltrated via log aggregation systems, monitoring dashboards, or error reporting tools, enabling session hijacking. [verified: MISSING-CONTROL: logger.warning() at line 70 writes request.headers.get('authorization') in plaintext to application logs; no log redaction, filtering, or masking exists anywhere in the app, and _wrk_gate protects endpoint access but does not prevent sensitive data from being logged once the endpoint is reached.]

Missing authorization: field workers and dispatchers can view audit logs for any job without ownership/region check — A field worker or dispatcher can retrieve audit trail entries for arbitrary jobs, leaking IP addresses, user activity patterns, and operational metadata across tenant/region boundaries. [verified: The list_job_audit_logs endpoint queries AuditLog by job_id directly with only a role check (require_roles), never calling can_access_job to verify the requesting field_worker owns the job or the dispatcher covers the job's region — unlike every other job-scoped endpoint (jobs.py, messages.py, incidents.py, proofs.py) which all enforce can_access_job.]

User Enumeration via Registration Response — Attackers can build a list of valid email addresses for targeted phishing, credential stuffing, or password-reset attacks. [verified: The register endpoint (auth.py:30-31) returns distinct 'Email already registered' (HTTP 400) when the email exists vs. proceeding normally when it does not, enabling an attacker to enumerate valid registered email addresses.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints — Attackers can brute-force user passwords, enumerate valid accounts via timing, or spam password-reset emails without restriction. [verified: No rate-limiting library (slowapi), middleware, or per-endpoint throttle exists anywhere in the codebase — login, register, and password-reset endpoints have zero brute-force protection, allowing unlimited credential guessing.]

Auth Cookie Set with secure=False — Session cookies transmitted over HTTP are vulnerable to network interception and session hijacking via man-in-the-middle attacks. [verified: The login endpoint sets the access_token cookie with secure=False (auth.py:57) unconditionally, with no check against settings.ENVIRONMENT — the cookie will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP in any non-HTTPS deployment, exposing it to network interception.]

Denial of service via unbounded CSV file upload in import endpoints — An attacker with dispatcher credentials can exhaust server memory by uploading an extremely large CSV file, causing the application to crash or become unresponsive. [verified: Both import_customers (line 25) and import_jobs (line 89) call file.file.read() with no size check, and no request body size limit exists anywhere (no middleware, no uvicorn config, no FastAPI setting). The proofs upload endpoint has a 10MB check, proving size limits are an expected control. An authenticated dispatcher/ops_admin can upload an arbitrarily large CSV to exhaust memory.]

Missing Region Authorization for Dispatchers in Incident Detail — A dispatcher can view incident details (including internal_notes and resolution) for incidents outside their assigned regions, enabling cross-region data access. [verified: get_incident only checks authorization for customer and field_worker roles; dispatchers bypass all checks with no region-scoping via DispatcherRegion, even though the list_incidents endpoint on the same router does enforce region filtering and the can_access_job helper in dependencies.py already implements the correct dispatcher region check.]

Internal Notes Exposed to Customers via Job Detail Endpoint — Customers can read internal operational notes on their own jobs, violating data separation between customer-facing and internal fields. [verified: get_job returns JobOut (includes internal_notes) after can_access_job only checks customer ownership — no field-level filtering strips internal_notes for customers. The developer acknowledges the same gap in incidents.py:148-152 with a pass/no-op, confirming no compensating control exists.]

Missing Region Authorization for Dispatchers in Message Listing — A dispatcher can read all internal messages across all regions, violating the regional scope boundary defined by DispatcherRegion assignments. [verified: list_messages has no DispatcherRegion-based filter for dispatchers — the if/elif block (lines 26-43) covers only customer and field_worker, leaving dispatchers with unfiltered access to all messages. Similar regional scoping exists in incidents.py:59-62 and jobs.py:59-63, confirming the control is intentionally required but absent here.]

Unrestricted file upload with no content-type or extension validation — Attacker can upload malicious files (e.g., HTML, scripts) that are served directly from /uploads, enabling stored XSS or phishing via the app's own domain. [verified: The upload endpoint at proofs.py:67 validates only file size (10MB); it performs no MIME-type allowlisting, extension whitelisting, or content inspection, and preserves the attacker-supplied extension in the saved path. Uploaded files are served directly via StaticFiles mount at /uploads (main.py:56), so an authenticated worker can upload an .html file that executes arbitrary JavaScript in the app]

CSV Formula Injection in Export Functions — Arbitrary command execution on the machine of anyone opening the exported CSV in spreadsheet software if formula-prefixed data exists in the database [verified: csv_response at reports.py:19 writes cells via csv.DictWriter with zero formula-prefix (=,+,-,@) sanitization; attacker-controlled full_name (RegisterRequest full_name: str, no validators) and CSV-imported company_name flow from DB into exports consumed by ops_admin/dispatcher — no input validation or output escaping anywhere in the chain.]

Missing Security Headers on All Responses — Clients lack protection against MIME-type sniffing, clickjacking, and downgrade attacks. [verified: No security headers middleware exists anywhere in the codebase (no HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, or CSP are set on any response). Only CORS middleware is present. These are genuinely absent defense-in-depth controls with low standalone impact.]
